Abstract
Hydrogel-based flexible sensors combine tissue-like mechanical properties with superior sensing performance,
showing immense potential in human–machine interactions, soft robotics, and health monitoring. Although
significant progress has been made in related research, the fabrication of precise structures, the environmental
tolerance of materials, and the heterogeneous integration between materials and devices remain key research
challenges. In response to these challenges, this review provides a comprehensive review of the latest progress
in hydrogel-based sensors, covering the entire process from material fabrication and functional regulation to
interface engineering. First, the impacts of advanced processing techniques such as solution processing,
microstructure molding, photolithography, additive manufacturing, and fiber spinning on film structure are
discussed in detail. Subsequently, physicochemical strategies for enhancing sensing performance and
environmental tolerance are analyzed. Furthermore, diverse assembly schemes and interface engineering
strategies are highlighted. Finally, typical applications in pressure, strain, environmental, and physiological
signal monitoring are summarized. This review aims to provide guidance for the development of next-
generation high-performance and stable flexible electronic systems.

1. Introduction
With the rapid advancement of the internet of things (IoT), artificial intelligence (AI), and personalised
medicine, modern information technology is undergoing a paradigm shift from rigid devices to flexible
electronics. In cutting-edge fields such as human‒machine interaction (HMI)[1], soft robotics[2], and health
monitoring[3], developing high-performance sensing materials that seamlessly conform to dynamic skin and
exhibit tissue-like mechanical properties has become pivotal for bridging the digital world with biological
systems. Owing to their unique physicochemical structure, hydrogels have emerged as the core material for
constructing next-generation flexible interfaces[4, 5].
Hydrogels, defined as three-dimensional (3D) hydrophilic polymer networks, are widely present in
natural systems, including plants, animals, and microorganisms[6, 7]. The developmental timeline of the
hydrogels is illustrated in Figure 1. The term “hydrogel” was first proposed in 1894 by Van Bemmelen,
initiating scientific interest in this material[8]. After decades of research, Wichterle and Lim successfully
synthesized poly(2-hydroxyethyl methacrylate) hydrogels in 1960 and developed the first biocompatible soft
contact lenses based on this material, marking a significant advancement in hydrogel research and
applications[9]. This breakthrough signifies a shift in research focus from material exploration to performance
optimization, thereby facilitating the development of hydrogels with conductivity, stimulus-responsive
properties, and adhesive capabilities[10–15]. These materials demonstrate biomimetic flexibility and
permeability comparable to those of biological tissues, showing remarkable potential in biomedical
applications such as wound healing[16], drug release[17], and tissue engineering[18, 19]. With advancements in
materials science and flexible electronics, hydrogel applications have expanded to include sensors[19–29],
supercapacitors[13, 30, 31], and bioelectrodes[32, 33]. Such mechanical compliance and sensitivity to external
stimuli (e.g., pressure, strain, and temperature) enable innovative solutions for health monitoring and human–
machine interfaces. Post-2020, hydrogel development entered a new phase characterized by interdisciplinary
integration and AI, facilitating the emergence of hydrogels in cutting-edge fields, including smart
healthcare[34–37], bionic electronic skin[38–43], and soft robotics[44–47].
Currently, numerous reviews have been published concerning hydrogels in the field of flexible
electronics. For instance, a review on hydrogel-based flexible electronics was presented[48]. This review
primarily focused on the latest synthetic methods for advanced functional hydrogels and corresponding
cutting-edge applications across various domains, with a particular emphasis on the correlation between

constitutes the core motivation for this review. First, the bulk synthesis of hydrogels via simple cast-film

by next-generation sensors. Second, synergistically optimising synthetic strategies and encapsulation
techniques to confer structural integrity and functional stability across diverse environments remains an urgent
manufacturing challenge[52]. Moreover, the fabrication of flexible sensors inherently involves a cross-scale
heterogeneous integration process. The unique ‘soft and wet’ properties of hydrogels result in significant
mechanical mismatches with rigid electrodes and encapsulation layers[53, 54]. The establishment of robust
heterogeneous interfaces during manufacturing to prevent delamination and failure under dynamic loads
represents a major technical bottleneck in current device processing.

and systematically investigates hydrogel synthesis techniques, functional tuning strategies, sensor assembly
processes, application domains, as well as current challenges and future development trends (see Figure 2).

manufacturing techniques for hydrogels, encompassing solution processing, microstructure molding,
photolithography, additive manufacturing, and fiber spinning, which serve as the cornerstone for achieving

2. Fabrication techniques for hydrogels
Previous gelation strategies have established foundational physicochemical principles for hydrogel formation,
yet traditional bulk synthesis alone cannot meet the complex demands of next-generation flexible electronics.
In human‒machine interfaces and soft robotics, devices must achieve seamless conformal contact with
irregular biological tissues, provide precise mechanical feedback, and adapt their morphology in dynamic
environments. These advanced capabilities require multi-scale structural engineering beyond simple gelation
control. The fabrication techniques define not only hydrogel shape accuracy but also pore architecture and
orientation to determine device sensitivity, linearity, and anisotropic response. This section systematically
reviews key hydrogel structural design paradigms from a manufacturing perspective, covering solution
processing, microstructure molding, photolithography, additive manufacturing, and fiber spinning.
2.1. Solution processing
Solution processing is the most fundamental and versatile strategy for hydrogel preparation. Its core process
involves precursor composition regulation and liquid‒solid transition. To introduce functional components
and regulate formulations, four main technical routes exist: physical casting, one-pot in-situ polymerization,
solvent exchange, and dip-coating.
Physical casting is the most intuitive method with the lowest technical barrier. It is primarily suitable for
pre-synthesized water-soluble high molecular weight polymers, such as polyvinyl alcohol (PVA), gelatin,
sodium alginate (SA), or chitosan (CS)[55, 56]. This process involves dissolving polymer powder in a solvent
(e.g., water, organic solvents, etc.) to form a homogeneous solution, which is then cast onto a mold or substrate.
Subsequently, physical methods like freeze-thaw or cooling induce a liquid‒solid transition for shaping
(Figure 3(a)). In contrast to casting methods based on macromolecular physical assembly, one-pot in-situ
polymerization allows for the direct construction of crosslinked networks from a precursor mixture of
monomers, crosslinkers, initiators, and solvents. As shown in Figure 3(b), a single step of irradiation or thermal
treatment triggers free radical polymerization, thereby inducing rapid solidification and obviating the need for
complex post-processing[57, 58]. This process not only precisely replicates micro/nano textures from molds
while maintaining high coating flatness but also ensures the uniformity of the polymer network at the
microscopic scale[59]. Based on the principles of in-situ polymerization, the HSCP hydrogel was fabricated by
ultraviolet (UV) irradiation of a mixture containing acrylamide (AM), honey, NaCl, the crosslinker N,N’-
methylene diacrylamide (MBA), and a photoinitiator for 45 min, yielding a network with excellent self-

adhesion, conductivity, and antibacterial properties[60]. When monomers are water-insoluble or specific
functional assemblies are needed, the solvent exchange strategy serves as a versatile method for structural
shaping and functionalization. A typical strategy involves the initial formation of an organogel network in an
organic solvent, followed by immersion of the resultant gel in water. During this stage, a concentration
gradient drives solvent exchange, wherein the progressive displacement of the organic solvent by water
induces phase separation or reorganization of the polymer chains, ultimately yielding a hydrogel (Figure
3(c))[61, 62]. Additionally, by immersing the preformed hydrogel in a solution containing functional components,
solvent permeation can fill these components into the interstitial spaces of the polymer network[63–65]. Such a
diffusion-based post-processing method can avoid the inhibition of polymerization reactions by strong
oxidants or high-concentration ions. For example, a smart adaptive ZL-PAM hydrogel was prepared by
soaking pre-formed PAM hydrogel in ZnSO4 and LiBr solutions to introduce Zn2+ and Li+. Hygroscopic Li+
provides excellent moisturizing ability, while Zn2+ suppresses byproducts (Zn(OH)2) and modulates water
content. It enables reversible switching between water-rich and water-deficient states for crosstalk-free dual
sensing of oxygen and humidity in a single device[64]. Similarly, a PAM/Ca-Alg double-network hydrogel
fiber was also fabricated via a soaking strategy. The fibers were sequentially immersed in CaCl2 and LiBr
solutions to form an ionically crosslinked network and introduce hygroscopic Li+ and Br– ions, achieving
excellent mechanical properties and drying and freezing tolerance[65]. As a complement to the aforementioned
strategies, dip-coating offers a pathway for the fabrication of thin and integrated hydrogels by incorporating
prefabricated scaffolds. This method involves immersing high-porosity nanonetworks (such as nanofiber
membranes or porous scaffolds) into a hydrogel precursor solution, utilizing micro/nanoscale capillary effects
to drive rapid infiltration and wetting of the framework. Subsequently, through appropriate physical or
chemical curing processes, a morphologically uniform and ultrathin hydrogel is formed under the physical
confinement of the nanoscaffold (Figure 3(d))[66]. Specifically, through this approach, organohydrogel
nanofilms with a thickness of only 392 nm were prepared by infiltrating polyurethane (PU) nanonetworks
with a gelatin-glycerol (Gly) precursor solution[67]. These nanofilm electrodes exhibited exceptional skin
conformability and environmental stability, enabling continuous and stable electrocardiogram (ECG)
monitoring for up to 9 days. This approach not only overcomes the thickness control limitations inherent in
traditional casting methods but also leverages the mechanical reinforcement of the nanonetwork to enhance
the structural integrity of the film, resulting in hydrogels with superior flexibility and ultrathin characteristics.

Once the precursor is prepared, fluid processing techniques convert it into specific geometries for
designated applications. Conventional casting enables tunable hydrogel thickness from micrometers to
millimeters via dimensionally customized molds (Figure 4(a)). Spin coating uses centrifugal force to spread
the precursors into uniform microscale films (Figure 4(b)). Spray coating employs high-pressure atomization
for directional deposition, making it ideal for creating functional coatings on substrates (Figure 4(c)).
Regarding spin-coating applications, hydrogel thin films with controllable thicknesses have been successfully
fabricated[68]. A polyacrylamide (PAM)/carrageenan hydrogel film with tunable thickness (54.61–85.72 μm)
was fabricated by spin-coating the precursor onto oxygen plasma-treated polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS)
substrates at speeds of 250–1 000 rpm. In another approach, a modified spin-coating strategy was employed
to fabricate an ionogel-based humidity sensor array, producing uniform sensing films with thicknesses down
to 2.4 μm and achieving ultrafast response/recovery times of 0.65 s/0.85 s[69]. Spray coating not only is widely
used for the rapid prototyping of hydrogel wound dressings and the construction of surface conductive layers,
but also serves as an important method for fabricating high-performance gel thin films. Further investigations
have demonstrated the efficacy of spray coating in developing flexible sensing interfaces[70]. In this approach,
a mixture of polymer matrices and functional solvents is atomized and deposited onto heated substrates.
Precise regulation of the spray pressure and duration facilitates the rapid formation of uniform and dense gel
networks. Sensors fabricated via this process retain the advantages of simple operation and easy patterning.

photolithography are currently the most widely used surface micromachining techniques. Molding primarily

relies on pre-fabricated master templates, which can be precision-made via lithographic silicon wafers or laser
etching, or directly replicated from textured materials. The typical process involves casting a formulated
hydrogel precursor onto the template surface. After physical or chemical gelation, demolding transfers the
template’s topographic features with high fidelity to the hydrogel surface. The essence of such microstructural
design lies in altering the mechanical conduction path of the device. Structures such as micro-pyramids,
micropillar arrays, or interlocked geometries exhibit nonlinear changes in contact area and generate localized
stress concentrations under compression[71]. This geometric enhancement enables sensors to produce
significant signal variations even under extremely low pressure, effectively overcoming the sensitivity
limitations of conventional flat films. As shown in Figure 4(d), an AM/agarose/NaCl ionic hydrogel was
fabricated using a commercial anti-micropyramid template. The micro-pyramid structure significantly
enhanced the capacitive sensing performance through stress concentration, achieving a high sensitivity of 172
kPa–1 within 30 kPa, a fast response time of 11.2 ms, and a low detection limit of 0.5 Pa[72]. Furthermore, to
reduce process costs and optimize demolding, secondary transfer strategies based on soft molds are widely
adopted. Researchers often use low-surface-energy silicone elastomers such as PDMS or Ecoflex to replicate
precision photolithographic silicon wafers or naturally textured biological surfaces into flexible intermediate
molds. Hydrogel precursors are then cast into these flexible molds[73]. This approach not only protects delicate
master templates from mechanical damage during repeated operations but also leverages the inherent low
surface energy and excellent elastic deformation of soft molds to significantly reduce interfacial adhesion and
facilitate demolding after gelation. Consequently, it ensures microstructural integrity while enabling efficient
mold reuse. In contrast, photolithography utilizes photochemical reactions to achieve higher-resolution
patterning, employing photoinitiators sensitive to specific wavelengths and photomasks to regulate the spatial
distribution of UV light. Exposed regions undergo crosslinking and solidification, while unexposed areas
remain liquid and are washed away, thereby constructing high-density micro-nano structures[74]. A
representative strategy utilized direct microlithography for the fabrication of high-density gel-skins. The key
innovation lay in creating a photosensitive gel material and realizing a patterning process without photoresist.
By employing a mask to selectively expose and develop the gel precursor under UV light, high-precision gel
arrays were directly produced, which significantly streamlined the complex procedures of traditional
photolithography (Figure 4(e))[75]. Such a strategy successfully produced high-density flexible electronic skin,
offering new insights for efficient device integration.

2.3. Additive manufacturing
Additive manufacturing technology fabricates complex 3D hydrogel structures by digital model control and
layer-by-layer stacking, greatly expanding design freedom. Among these, direct ink writing (DIW) printing,
which is the most widely used extrusion-based technique, relies on micro-nozzles to extrude hydrogel inks
with tunable rheological properties. Recent advances reveal that the high shear flow field inside the nozzle
can induce the alignment of anisotropic particles or nanoreinforcing phases along the printing path[76, 77]. For
instance, a composite ink containing conductive ceramic flakes (~200 nm thick) was extruded through a 35
mm-long cylindrical nozzle[78]. Shear forces during printing induced highly oriented alignment of the flake
fillers, yielding composite organohydrogel monofilaments with concentric layered microstructures. These
monofilaments were further printed into biomimetic macroscopic architectures such as unidirectional arrays,
endowing the material with significant anisotropy (Figure 4(f)). Notably, controlling the surface tension of
hydrogel ink is crucial; excessive surface tension can cause droplet splashing or satellite droplet formation
during jetting, severely degrading the edge sharpness and resolution of printed patterns. As a representative of
photocuring, digital light processing (DLP) printing offers higher forming accuracy (~20–250 μm) than DIW
printing does[79, 80]. This technology uses digital projection to cure photosensitive precursors layer by layer via
area exposure, enabling internal interconnected micropores or overhanging structures that are difficult to
achieve with extrusion-based methods. DLP printing materials typically consist of photoactive polymers,
photoinitiators, and photoabsorbers[81]. By adjusting the content and ratio of the first two components, the
mechanical properties of DLP-printed hydrogels can be tailored. The photoabsorber also plays a critical role,
as it influences the printing resolution during the photopolymerization process[82, 83]. For instance, DLP
printing was utilized to fabricate organohydrogels with tailored architectures, such as diamond, grid, and
peanut-like geometries[84]. The resulting ionic and electronic hydrogels exhibited remarkable stability,
yielding gauge factors of 4.5 (0%–200% strain) and 13.5/1.5 × 106 (0%–2%/2%–100% strain), respectively.
A 3D grid structure sensor printed and integrated into an HMI system achieved precise control with a minimum
monitoring angle of 5° (Figure 4(g)). To further improve the microstructural resolution of sensors, two-photon
polymerization employs femtosecond lasers based on nonlinear absorption. This technique achieves feature
sizes from the micrometer scale down to below 100 nm, albeit with long fabrication times (hours) and limited
construction dimensions. For example, researchers have used this technique to fabricate photonic crystal
hydrogel microsensors within microfluidic chips. The sensors achieve submicron resolution (16 μm diameter)

2.4. Fiber spinning
Processing hydrogels into one-dimensional continuous fibers is key for wearable smart textile integration. Wet
spinning, as the process for hydrogel fiber production, involves extruding a polymer dope through a spinneret
into a coagulation bath. During this process, the extruded jet undergoes diffusion or rapid ionic crosslinking,
inducing instantaneous phase separation and solidification into nascent fibers. Subsequent mechanical
drawing further promotes molecular chain alignment along the fiber axis, enhancing mechanical strength[88,
89]. As illustrated in Figure 4(h), bioinspired aligned hydrogels were fabricated via a wet-spinning strategy.
This process involved injecting a mixed solution of PVA, polydopamine (PDA)-carbon nanotubes (CNTs),
and poly(3,4-ethylenedioxythiophene) polystyrene sulfonate (PEDOT: PSS) into an ammonium sulfate
coagulation bath. The shear flow generated during extrusion facilitated the alignment of the polymer chains,
resulting in the formation of fibrous filaments. These fibers were then immersed in a sodium pyrrolidone
carboxylic acid (PCA-Na) solution, where salt ions promoted interchain aggregation and crystallization,

2.5. Challenges in the fabrication techniques of hydrogels
2.5.1. Trade-off between processing precision and manufacturing throughput. An inherent conflict exists
between microscale structural control and scalable production efficiency. High-resolution features like
submicron patterns and complex 3D architectures are critical for sensitivity but typically rely on high-
precision techniques that increase cost and reduce throughput. Photonic patterning (e.g., photolithography,
DLP) enables precise crosslinking but requires strict control and multi-step processing, limiting efficiency[107].
Conversely, high-throughput methods such as casting, spin coating, and injection molding offer scalability but
are constrained by rheology and diffusion to resolutions of tens or hundreds of micrometers; molding also
involves costly tooling and potential demolding damage[94]. This conflict reflects a systemic challenge
balancing material rheology, structural control, equipment complexity, and cost. Achieving structural accuracy
alongside high efficiency, low cost, and scalability remains a major hurdle for practical sensor manufacturing.
2.5.2. Trade-off between structural complexity and mechanical properties. The pursuit of structural
complexity—such as high-aspect-ratio microarrays, porous networks, or oriented fibers—enhances sensitivity
and deformability but often compromises polymer network integrity and stress transfer, reducing mechanical
robustness. High-aspect-ratio structures risk stress concentration and collapse; porous lattices weaken
connectivity and strength; and oriented fibers induce excessive anisotropy, limiting adaptability. Maintaining
mechanical reliability while increasing complexity remains a key challenge. Several mitigation strategies have
been proposed, including energy-dissipation networks[113], nanofiller or phase-separation reinforcement[114],
bioinspired structures for crack deflection[115], and post-treatment to regulate anisotropy and interfacial
bonding[116–119]. These approaches improve local performance but may introduce interfacial incompatibility
or long-term instability. The development of multiscale synergistic designs that integrate structural complexity
with intrinsic material reinforcement remains essential for achieving both functional performance and
mechanical reliability.
2.5.3. Trade-off between precision manufacturing and multiscale integration.
The trade-off originates from the conflict between constructing multiscale functional structures and
maintaining overall system stability. Integrating micro/nanoscale functional layers with macroscopic flexible
substrates often leads to interfacial stress, adhesion failure, and structural discontinuity due to material
mismatches. High-modulus layers may increase signal accuracy but risk delamination from soft substrates,
whereas prioritizing flexibility can compromise microstructural integrity. Multi-material fabrication
inconsistencies, including mismatches in curing, swelling, and thermal expansion, further induce residual

3. Strategies for designing hydrogel properties
While traditional hydrogels successfully mimic biological soft tissues in terms of water content and
mechanical modulus, they remain intrinsically passive materials composed of inert polymer networks. The
inherent electrical insulation, susceptibility to environmental fluctuations (including freezing, dehydration,
and swelling), irreversible mechanical damage, and chemical inertness at bio-interfaces constitute the core
bottlenecks restricting their application in next-generation flexible electronic devices. The essence of
functional design lies in overcoming these intrinsic limitations through molecular engineering and
microstructure regulation, thereby endowing the materials with active sensing capabilities and environmental
adaptability. This section systematically analyzes the structural design logic of high-performance sensing
hydrogels from four critical dimensions: the construction strategies for conductive networks, adaptability
design for extreme environments, self-healing strategies, and biocompatibility and antibacterial properties.
3.1. Construction strategies for conductive networks
Imparting excellent charge transport capabilities to insulating polymer networks is a prerequisite for realizing
sensing functionalities. Current strategies primarily face a core trade-off: how to introduce highly conductive
phases without compromising the intrinsic flexibility and high water content of hydrogels. Depending on the
charge carrier type, this field has evolved into two distinct technical routes: electronic conduction and ionic
conduction. These approaches encompass diverse functional units, ranging from traditional conductive
polymers (CPs) and metal- and carbon-based fillers to emerging materials such as MXenes and ion-based
fillers (Figure 5(a)).
Electron-conductive hydrogels：Electron-conductive hydrogels rely primarily on conductive fillers to
form a physical percolation network within the polymer matrix. Their performance is governed by the intrinsic
conductivity of the fillers, the dispersion state of these fillers, and the interfacial interactions with the matrix.
CPs, represented by polyaniline (PANI)[120–122], polypyrrole (PPy)[123, 124], and PEDOT:PSS[125, 126], achieve
charge transport through the effective delocalization of conjugated π-electron structures along the polymer
backbone[127]. Compared with rigid inorganic fillers, CPs offer superior organic compatibility, flexibility, and
ease of processing. However, hydrophobic conductive chains are prone to macroscopic phase separation

migration for charge transport. Their soft and wet characteristics closely mimic those of biological tissues,

5(f))[81]. This phase-separated structure not only achieved an ultra-high ionic conductivity of 0.0323 S·cm–1

such structured ion channel designs. This approach aims to balance electrical performance with optical and
mechanical properties while leveraging the wide liquid range of ILs to endow materials with additional
environmental adaptability.

3.2. Adaptability design for extreme environments
The presence of water in hydrogels is a double-edged sword. While it maintains the material’s flexibility and
conductivity, it also leads to freezing at low temperatures, hardening due to water loss in dry environments,
and excessive swelling underwater. Therefore, structural design at the molecular level to disrupt the hydrogen
bond network of water or limit its permeation is key to ensuring stable device operation under all weather
conditions.
Anti-freezing and water-retention strategies: addressing freezing and evaporation primarily involves
thermodynamically disrupting the tetrahedral hydrogen bond network of free water or lowering its vapor
pressure. In hydrogels, water primarily exists as thermodynamically unstable “free water”, which freezes
readily at low temperatures and evaporates rapidly in dry environments due to high vapor pressure[158, 159].
These phenomena lead to material hardening and the loss of electrical conductivity. Consequently, the design
of anti-freezing and water-retention hydrogels relies on the introduction of electrolytes with strong hydration
capacity (inorganic salts[160, 161], zwitterions[162, 163]), strong hydrogen-bond donor/acceptor solvents (organic
solvents[164, 165], acidic substances[166, 167], deep eutectic solvents (DESs)[168]), bulky asymmetric ionic solvents
(ILs)[154] or specific biomacromolecules[169]. These components utilize ion‒dipole interactions, hydrogen-bond
competition, steric hindrance, or interfacial adsorption to increase the bound water ratio and lower the
chemical potential of the solvent system. Such interventions inhibit the ordered arrangement of water
molecules and ice nucleation while effectively suppressing moisture loss[170], ensuring signal stability in the
cold or arid environments of hydrogel-based sensors.
Utilizing the colligative properties generated by high concentrations of inorganic salts is a classic and
cost-effective strategy. Various metal ions, including Li+, Na+, Zn2+, Ca2+, and Fe3+, have proven effective[160,
161, 171, 172]. In a representative study, the synergy between LiCl and a polymer network was exploited to develop
PMS hydrogels. The strong hydration of Cl− and Li+ disrupted the hydrogen bonds of free water, enabling the
material to remain flexible at ultralow temperatures of −80 ℃. Differential scanning calorimetry confirmed

Anti-swelling strategies: in underwater or high-humidity application scenarios, the unrestricted swelling
of hydrophilic polymer networks leads to increased free volume, diluted ion concentration, and reduced
mechanical strength. This consequently causes severe signal drift and structural failure. Therefore,
constructing an inherently anti-swelling hydrogel system is essential for maintaining performance stability in
such wet environments. Unlike device-level strategies that rely on external physical encapsulation (discussed
in Section 4.3), material-level anti-swelling designs introduce two molecular-scale constraint mechanisms to
counteract osmotic pressure-driven swelling. On the one hand, reducing the network’s affinity for water by
adjusting the hydrophilic–hydrophobic balance (e.g., via solvent exchange or hydrophobic modification)
drives a transition from a hydrophilic swollen state to a hydrophobic compact state, thereby
thermodynamically suppressing swelling. On the other hand, the construction of crosslinked structures with
high elastic recovery by increasing the crosslink density effectively resists swelling induced by chemical
potential gradients. These strategies limit water molecule migration across interfaces, thereby fundamentally
ensuring the stability of hydrogel-based sensors in aqueous environments. The following details the solvent
exchange, hydrophobic modification, and high crosslink density strategies involved.
The solvent exchange strategy utilizes the polarity difference between good and poor solvents to
modulate polymer chain conformation[108]. When a gel is transferred from a good solvent to a poor one, chain‒
chain interactions dominate over chain‒solvent interactions. This drives the molecular chains to undergo
microphase separation and collapse into a dense physically cross-linked network. This process shifts the gel
from a hydrophilic swollen state to a hydrophobic compact state, thereby thermodynamically suppressing
swelling. Specifically, a DMSO-to-water solvent exchange strategy was implemented to induce controlled
aggregation of the hydrophobic segments, yielding a swelling ratio of 4.79% (Figure 7(a))[61]. Furthermore,
such an approach facilitates the fabrication of high-strength exogels, with the primary advantage being the
attainment of exceptional mechanical strength[189]. However, excessive network densification may
compromise stretchability and ion transport rates. Therefore, precise control over the degree of exchange is
essential.
Hydrophobic modification strategy offers a direct route for constructing endogenous barriers by
leveraging the entropy-driven aggregation of hydrophobic groups[190]. The introduced hydrophobic groups
spontaneously aggregate to minimize contact with water molecules, thereby significantly reducing the
material’s affinity for water and enhancing its inherent hydrophobicity. For instance, high-density hydrophobic

brittleness, decrease stretchability, and weaken interfacial adhesion. Therefore, a key challenge for practical

as flexibility, stretchability, adhesion, and biocompatibility.

3.3. Self-healing strategies
During the long-term operation of flexible electronic devices, repeated mechanical deformation inevitably
induces microcracks in hydrogel networks, leading to conductive pathway disruption and device failure.
Endowing hydrogels with self-healing capabilities essentially involves incorporating dynamic bonds that can
dissipate energy and undergo reversible reorganization, enabling spontaneous functional recovery through
molecular chain diffusion and re-entanglement at damaged interfaces. Current design strategies primarily
focus on dynamic covalent bonds, non-covalent interactions, and their synergistic effects.
Self-healing strategies based on dynamic covalent bonds enable hydrogel self-healing through reversible
chemical bonding, where covalent bonds can reform after breaking[211]. Common chemical motifs include
imine bonds[212], acylhydrazone bonds[213], borate ester bonds[153], disulfide bonds[214], and Diels-Alder (DA)
reactions[215] (Figure 8(a)). Imine bonds, formed via reversible condensation between amines and carbonyl
compounds (e.g., aldehydes and ketones), exhibit dynamic covalent characteristics. Owing to their reversible
equilibrium properties, they are widely utilized to fabricate self-healing hydrogels[216, 217]. In 2011, a
breakthrough study demonstrated rapid gelation of hydrogels based on the Schiff-base reaction and discovered
that the dynamic crosslinking mechanism endowed the hydrogels with self-healing properties. This finding
subsequently attracted widespread attention[218]. Acylhydrazone bonds are established through the reversible
condensation of hydrazines with aldehydes/ketones. While the formation mechanism is analogous to that of
imine bonds, acylhydrazone linkages exhibit enhanced stability[213]. Consequently, acidic conditions or
thermal stimuli are typically required to facilitate the dynamic reversibility of acylhydrazone bonds, thereby
enabling self-healing properties within the hydrogel[219, 220]. In boron-based systems, electron-deficient boron
atoms in boronic acid (or its derivatives) form reversible boronic ester bonds with cis-diols[221, 222]. These
dynamic bonds undergo continuous reversible rearrangement near damaged regions, maintaining structural
equilibrium and self-healing capacity. For instance, through the integration of dynamic boronic ester bond
exchange and physical ball milling, the fabricated PMP hydrogel exhibited nearly 100% mechanical recovery
within 120 s at room temperature. These results demonstrate the significant potential of dynamic boronic ester
bonds for rapid reconstruction[223]. Disulfide bonds, as another representative class of dynamic covalent bonds,
derive their dynamic characteristics primarily from exchange reactions triggered by thermal, UV, or redox
stimuli. Under external stimulation, disulfide bonds at the fracture interface undergo homolysis or thiol–
disulfide exchange reactions, which induce dynamic reorganization of the polymer network, thereby achieving
self-healing[224]. Owing to their excellent compatibility with polymer matrices, the integration of disulfide

ring structures through the reaction between a diene and a dienophile. Its inherent dynamic reversibility

Therefore, designing such materials requires carefully balancing dynamic activity with environmental stability
to suit complex application scenarios.
Unlike covalent bonds that require specific stimuli, self-healing hydrogels based on non-covalent
interactions rely primarily on dynamic reversible physical forces with low activation energies, enabling
autonomous healing at room temperature. These non-covalent interactions primarily include hydrogen
bonds[227], metal coordination[228], ionic interactions[229], host‒guest interaction[230], and hydrophobic
association (Figure 8(b))[194]. Hydrogen bonds represent the most fundamental mechanism. With a bond
energy of ~42 kJ·mol−1, it lies thermodynamically between van der Waals forces and strong chemical
bonds[231]. The picosecond-scale dissociation and recombination kinetics allow for instantaneous repair.
However, hydrogels composed solely of hydrogen bonds suffer from relatively low mechanical strength.
Furthermore, the post self-healing properties of such hydrogels are highly susceptible to environmental
conditions (such as temperature, humidity, pH, etc.), often resulting in structural failure or fracture. In contrast,
metal‒coordination bonds provide hydrogels with both structural stability and dynamic reversibility through
Lewis acid‒base interactions. Specifically, oxygen/nitrogen-containing functional groups (e.g., carboxyl,
catechol, and amino groups) within the network act as Lewis bases by donating electron pairs, while metal
ions (e.g., Ca2+, Al3+, Fe3+, and Zr4+) serve as Lewis acids by accepting electrons, forming coordination cross-
linking points[232, 233]. This bonding not only significantly enhances the mechanical strength of hydrogels but
also enables self-healing of damaged interfaces through reversible dissociation and reconstruction without the
need for external stimuli. The PAA-Fe3+ hydrogels utilized this mechanism to achieve self-healing[228]. Ionic
interactions construct dynamic cross-linked networks through electrostatic attraction between charged
polymers and counter-ions (polymers, ions, and nanomaterials)[229, 234–237]. The healing mechanism relies on
the redistribution of free ions at the fracture interface and the restoration of charge balance. Owing to its higher
bond energy than hydrogen bonds, this mechanism can enhance both the mechanical strength and the
performance stability of self-healing hydrogels. Furthermore, ionic interactions include ion‒dipole[238] and
dipole‒dipole interactions[239]. Ionic crosslinking is simple and efficient, yet it remains susceptible to charge

repeated damage[247]. These findings highlight the pivotal role of multi-dynamic interactions in hydrogel
design. Through further optimization of their synergistic effects, it is expected that more functional and
practical self-healing materials can be developed.

application. Biocompatibility ensures that materials maintain functionality without eliciting toxicity,
inflammation, or immune rejection during interactions with biological systems, while antibacterial properties
safeguard application safety through pathogen elimination. These characteristics originate from two intrinsic
attributes: (1) the high water content allows it to remain moist in contact with biological tissues without
causing dryness or irritation, (2) properties similar to those of the natural extracellular matrix promote cell
attachment, proliferation, and differentiation[248, 249]. Hydrogels with biocompatibility are typically composed

conductivity and mechanical properties. Future solutions may involve smart stimulus-responsive systems (e.g.,

3.5. Challenges in strategies for designing hydrogel properties
3.5.1. Trade-off among high conductivity, mechanical properties, and biocompatibility. Integrating high
conductivity, robust mechanics, and biocompatibility requires a systematic balance among conductive
components, network architecture, and biosafety. Electronic conductors (e.g., CPs and graphene) can
significantly enhance conductivity; however, filler aggregation, insufficient surface functionalization, or
residual impurities may induce cytotoxicity and increase the local modulus, thereby compromising mechanical
matching with tissues[133, 251]. Metallic fillers achieve ultrahigh conductivity (up to 1 739 S·cm−1) but risk
metal ion release (e.g., Ag+)[134]. LMs exhibit excellent electrical continuity and strain adaptability, with
elongations exceeding 2 000%, but they still face challenges such as poor wettability and leakage risk[252, 253].
Ionic conductors provide softness but high concentrations may disrupt the cellular osmotic balance. The data
summarized in Table 3 further reveal the performance distribution of different conductive systems in terms of
electrical conductivity and stretchability. Polymer-based hydrogels show the broadest conductivity range
(10−3–102 S·cm−1), with a maximum of 101.4 S·cm−1. Carbon-based systems typically range from 10−5 to 10−1
S·cm−1. Metal-based systems achieve the highest conductivity but exhibit relatively limited stretchability. In
contrast, ionic- and composite-based hydrogels present moderate conductivity while achieving high
elongation (>1 500%), indicating superior compliance. Overall, achieving high conductivity often relies on
high filler loading or dense conductive networks, which may compromise softness and biosafety. Conversely,
prioritizing mechanical and biological compatibility can restrict charge transport efficiency. Therefore,
achieving synergistic multifunctionality requires the construction of efficient and stable conductive pathways,
combined with network topology regulation, interfacial reinforcement, controlled filler distribution, and ion‒
electron synergistic transport design, to optimize performance while maintaining biocompatibility and
mechanical flexibility.

hydrophobic domains act as physical barriers that increase path tortuosity and ionic resistance. These large
hydrophobic clusters further reduce the transparency and induce significant hysteresis and residual strain[257].
Overcoming these antagonisms requires a shift from “functional stacking” to “functional decoupling.” Recent
advances demonstrate that inducing bicontinuous phase separation to create dual-continuous ion channels can
simultaneously enhance mechanical and electrochemical performance[62, 258]. This suggests that phase
separation is not inherently detrimental and that the key lies in the precise topological control of phase domains.
Consequently, the core future challenge is constructing multiscale hierarchical networks. By optimizing hybrid
crosslinking modes, network topology, and hydrophilic–hydrophobic balance, researchers should establish a
precise equilibrium between segmental mobility, structural stability, and energy dissipation.
3.5.3 Trade-off between multifunctional integration and long-term stability. Multifunctional hydrogels
integrate conductive units, reversible crosslinks, antimicrobial agents, and adaptive regulators to enable signal
transmission, self-healing, environmental adaptability, and biointerface control. However, long-term use risks
component migration, phase separation, or aggregation, disrupting network uniformity. Dynamic reversible
bonds support healing but may cause network rearrangement and stress relaxation, while stable covalent bonds
enhance durability but limit adaptability and healing[259]. Conductive pathways and functional additives may
suffer interfacial failure under repeated deformation, leading to signal drift[260]. Therefore, a fundamental
trade-off exists between dynamic tunability and long-term stability. Future designs should emphasize
multiscale topological engineering, synergistic stable-dynamic networks, and controlled anchoring of
functional components for sustained multifunctional performance.

4. Assembly and encapsulation design of hydrogel-based flexible sensors
Benefiting from the widespread application of advanced manufacturing techniques, such as solution
processing, microstructure molding, photolithography, additive manufacturing, and fiber spinning, high-
precision regulation has been achieved for the microscales and intrinsic physicochemical properties of
hydrogels. However, this represents only the initial stage in the development of practical sensing technologies.
The ultimate performance of hydrogel-based sensors depends not only on the physicochemical properties of
the materials themselves but is also significantly constrained by subsequent device engineering design.
Transforming soft, hydrated hydrogels with ionic conductivity into stable and reliable electronic devices is a
systematic engineering endeavor involving multiscale structural regulation and multiphysics coordination.
The core challenge lies in effectively bridging the significant disparities in mechanical modulus, conductive
mechanisms, and surface energy between hydrogels and conventional electronic components such as metal
electrodes, conductive wires, and encapsulation layers.
Specific device assembly strategies directly dictate the efficiency of stress transfer and the patterns of
electric field distribution, serving as the key to resolving the intrinsic trade-off between sensitivity and the
sensing range. Meanwhile, interface engineering acts as a bridge connecting ionic and electronic conductors,
where the quality of interfacial anchoring fundamentally governs the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) of signal
transduction and the long-term stability of the device. Advanced encapsulation techniques addressing the
inherent dehydration of hydrogels constitute the final safeguard for ensuring environmental adaptability. In
light of this, this section systematically explores the comprehensive fabrication chain of hydrogel sensors. It
begins by reviewing function-oriented device architectures and assembly strategies, proceeds to elaborate on
interface design principles for achieving robust and low-impedance connections, and concludes with a
discussion on encapsulation schemes for enhancing device robustness.
4.1. Assembly strategies
The assembly strategies of hydrogel-based flexible sensors serve as a pivotal bridge linking intrinsic material
properties to ultimate device performance. Fundamentally, this process involves engineering geometric
structures to modulate the transduction pathways from external stimuli to internal electrical signals, as well as
the distribution of physical fields. Driven by variations in monitoring targets and application scenarios, current
assembly strategies have evolved into five mainstream categories: vertical sandwich architecture, planar
interdigital architecture, core-shell encapsulation architecture, asymmetric bilayer architecture, and
monolithic architecture.

interdigitated electrodes constructed on a substrate via photolithography or printing technologies (Figure

4.2. Chemical anchoring and mechanical interlocking
Within the hierarchical architecture of hydrogel-based flexible sensors, the heterogeneous interfaces where
hydrogels contact metallic electrodes, elastomeric substrates, or conductive textiles serve as pivotal junctures
for determining both signal integrity and long-term stability. These interfaces also constitute high-risk zones
for stress concentration and failure. Owing to the substantial chemical potential difference and mechanical
modulus mismatch between soft, wet hydrogels and rigid, dry electronic materials, interfaces that rely solely
on van der Waals forces or simple physical adsorption are highly susceptible to delamination or slippage under
dynamic cyclic loading. Such interface failure not only causes dramatic fluctuations in contact resistance,
generating signal artifacts, but also disrupts ion‒electron conduction pathways, leading to complete functional
loss of the device. To resolve this inherent contradiction, current interface engineering strategies focus
primarily on two dimensions: constructing molecular-level covalent chemical bridges and developing micro-
nano-scale topological mechanical interlocking.
Covalent chemical bridging strategies aim to eliminate interfacial discontinuities at the molecular level
by introducing robust chemical bonds between heterogeneous materials through surface chemical
modification or in situ reactions. For instance, click chemistry principles can be utilized to establish strong
interfacial chemical bonds between hydrogels and substrate surfaces[294]. Specifically, the epoxy groups on the
hydrogel surface can react with the amino groups in bovine serum albumin to form robust covalent C‒N bonds.
This firmly anchors conductive films to the hydrogel substrates, achieving exceptionally high adhesion
strength at the interface. The resulting sensors withstand severe stretching and tens of thousands of fatigue
cycles, effectively resolving interlayer separation issues. Beyond surface modification, a universal in-situ
anchoring technique was developed (Figure 10(a))[260]. Researchers subjected elastic PU porous substrates and
metal electrodes to silane coupling agent self-assembly treatment, followed by in-situ polymerisation of
conductive hydrogels within the pores. During polymerisation initiation, the active groups of the silane
coupling agent undergo covalent cross-linking with the gel network, thereby establishing a robust integral
chemical bond between the hydrogel and the device substrate.
Unlike molecular-level strategies involving chemical bonding, the topological mechanical interlocking
approach focuses on leveraging the geometric confinement effects of micro- and nanostructures. By anchoring
hydrogels within the pores or fiber networks of substrates, this mechanism disperses stress and impedes crack

a universal solution for heterogeneous integration. A relatively common strategy involves permeating the

Specifically, an electrospun porous thermoplastic PU fibre network serves as the interlocking scaffold,

perfectly preserving the inherent softness and skin adhesion of the hydrogel. In summary, whether through
molecular chemical bonding or microstructural interlocking, interface design is progressively evolving
towards physicochemical synergistic reinforcement. This approach aims to endow flexible sensors with
interface robustness surpassing that of natural tissues, enabling them to withstand extreme mechanical
deformation and complex physiological environments.
Notably, although the strategies discussed above have significantly enhanced the initial adhesion strength
of heterogeneous interfaces (as summarized in Table 4), their long-term stability under dynamic fatigue and
extreme environments is critical for determining the operational lifetime of hydrogel-based sensors. Under
dynamic fatigue, interfacial damage proceeds via crack propagation. Interfaces relying solely on chemical
anchoring lack energy dissipation, causing cracks to initiate near-grafted bonds and propagate rapidly, limiting
fatigue life. In contrast, interfaces with mechanical interlocking or dynamic sacrificial bonds (e.g.,
coordination or hydrogen bonds) dissipate energy through anchorage friction or reversible bond
breakage/recombination, significantly retarding crack growth and enhancing fatigue resistance[297]. In humid
or aqueous environments, water molecules plasticize interfaces or hydrolyze susceptible bonds (e.g., ester
bonds), degrading adhesion[298]. Mitigation strategies include the use of hydrophobic barrier layers and
hydrolysis-resistant bonds such as amides or coordination bonds[299]. Under temperature fluctuations, the
coefficient of thermal expansion mismatches between hydrogels and rigid substrates accumulate thermal stress,
resulting in warping or delamination[300]. Mitigation strategies include introducing modulus gradient layers or
soft buffer layers to dissipate thermal stress and constructing thermally responsive, reversible bonds that
release stress through dynamic exchange upon temperature changes. Understanding the origins of these

Chemical anchoring and mechanical interlocking exhibit fundamental differences in stress transfer and
failure mechanisms. In terms of stress transfer, chemical anchoring relies on intermolecular forces (e.g.,
covalent or coordination bonds) across the interface. Stress is efficiently transmitted at the atomic scale
through these discrete bonds, enabling intimate contact without relative slippage. In contrast, mechanical
interlocking depends on interfacial geometric features such as microporous structures or topological
entanglements. Stress is transferred regionally at the micro/nano-scale through anchorage points by pushing
and friction, offering a buffering effect and enabling stress redistribution[301]. Regarding failure mechanisms,
chemical anchoring typically leads to brittle, catastrophic failure. Once the external force exceeds the bond
energy threshold, irreversible bond breakage occurs, rapidly initiating crack propagation and sudden
interfacial debonding[302]. Conversely, mechanical interlocking exhibits ductile, progressive failure. Under
stress, the anchorage points gradually deform and pull out, dissipating substantial energy through continuous
interfacial friction and material viscoelasticity, resulting in a slow failure process with clear precursors. This
fundamental distinction dictates that chemical anchoring is more suitable for high-sensitivity, small-
deformation sensing applications, whereas mechanical interlocking is preferable for flexible electronic devices
requiring high fatigue resistance, high deformation tolerance, and effective energy buffering.

4.3. Encapsulation strategies for environmental resistance
Although material modification strategies, such as the incorporation of organic solvents or ILs, as discussed
in Section 3.2, have significantly enhanced the intrinsic environmental tolerance of hydrogels, relying solely
on the stability of the material matrix often proves insufficient to fully withstand the erosion of extreme
environments in practical, long-term service scenarios. For instance, ILs may exhibit minimal exudation
during prolonged use, potentially triggering tissue inflammation[304]. Similarly, highly hygroscopic salts can
still absorb moisture gradually under extremely high humidity, leading to dimensional instability of the
device[305]. Therefore, from a device engineering perspective, constructing an external encapsulation system
capable of effectively and physically blocking the cross-interface transport of water molecules stands as a
primary prerequisite for ensuring the reliable functionality of hydrogel-based electronic devices in complex
and dynamic environments.
Current mainstream encapsulation strategies primarily revolve around establishing physical barriers.
Elastomer encapsulation is a widely adopted method, whose core mechanism involves constructing a dense
physical barrier around hydrogels using hydrophobic polymers such as silicone rubber or Ecoflex. This locks

Moreover, more robust interfacial chemical cross-linking strategies are frequently employed to achieve stable
connections between encapsulated elastomers and hydrogels. For instance, benzophenone is utilised to initiate
covalent bonds between the hydrogel surface and elastomer groups[307]. This ‘welded’ interface not only
endows the device with exceptional deformation resistance but also significantly enhances the water vapour
barrier efficiency through the formed covalent bond network.
While static encapsulation enhances stability, conventional elastomer coatings inevitably develop
microcracks under prolonged repeated stretching, leading to barrier failure. Inspired by the dynamic properties
of biological membranes, dynamic adaptive coatings offer a more sophisticated solution to fatigue failure
under deformation (Figure 11(b))[308]. This strategy mimics the fluid-mosaic model of cell membranes, centred
on constructing a dynamic, self-repairing protective layer. Within the coating, long-chain amphiphilic
molecules anchor to the hydrogel surface like membrane proteins, while the overlying lipid molecular layer
forms a dense hydrophobic barrier. The most ingenious design feature lies in preloading excess lipid molecules
within the hydrogel matrix. When surface coatings develop microscopic defects due to device deformation,
such as stretching or bending, these internal lipids migrate to the surface like repair molecules, dynamically
filling voids and restoring barrier integrity. This adaptive repair mechanism ensures sustained prevention of
water evaporation under both static and dynamic conditions, while maximally preserving the inherent
flexibility, conductivity, and even biocompatibility of the hydrogel. This offers a novel pathway towards
achieving long-term, reliable biointegrated electronic devices.
In summary, from developing elastomer encapsulation that forms static physical barriers to advancing
biomimetic coatings that provide dynamic adaptive protection, researchers are systematically addressing the
environmental stability challenges of hydrogel devices through multi-level mechanism innovations. These
strategies significantly expand their application potential in complex scenarios such as wearable electronics,
soft robotics, and biomedicine.

4.4.1 Interfacial failure mechanisms under multi-field coupling. The failure mechanisms of heterogeneous

fatigue, environmental stresses (e.g., osmotic swelling pressure, thermomechanical strain), and chemical
erosion. This knowledge gap makes it difficult to accurately predict the long-term service life of devices in
complex, dynamic real-world scenarios. Future research should employ in-situ, multi-modal characterization

development of physical failure models that describe the coupled mechanothermal‒electrochemical

4.4.2 Electrochemical instability of ion‒electron interfaces. The electrochemical stability of ion‒electron
conducting interfaces requires urgent improvement. During long-term cyclic deformation, microscopic
perturbations in the interfacial contact state can cause drastic drift in contact impedance. This induces
significant signal artifacts and baseline instability, severely compromising the fidelity of sensing signals.
Meanwhile, the high-concentration free ion environment within hydrogels poses a continuous electrochemical
corrosion risk to metal electrodes, leading to physical fracture and functional loss of conductive pathways[310].
Therefore, developing novel conductive interfacial layers that combine high mechanical compliance, strong
interfacial adhesion, and electrochemical inertness (such as introducing two-dimensional materials, CPs) is
critical for ensuring long-term device stability[311].
4.4.3 The functional paradox of encapsulation systems. The encapsulation system presents a prominent
functional paradox and design imbalance. The high dependence of hydrogels on moisture retention and the
rigid demand for physiological breathability in wearable applications constitute a fundamental performance
paradox. Existing encapsulation systems, while pursuing efficient prevention of water loss, often completely
block necessary gas and vapor exchange. This results in a functional design imbalance that not only severely
limits wearing comfort and physiological compatibility but also may cause skin inflammation due to localized
microenvironmental changes. The development of anisotropic or responsive encapsulation materials is
essential to achieve synergistic optimization of moisture retention and breathability[307].
5. Application in flexible electronics
The material synthesis strategies and device assembly architectures detailed in the preceding sections establish
a robust structural foundation for hydrogel-based sensors. However, the efficacy of these systems hinges on
their capacity to efficiently transduce multidimensional physical, chemical, or physiological stimuli into
quantifiable electrical signals. Despite the burgeoning diversity of application scenarios, the underlying signal
transduction mechanisms primarily operate via five fundamental principles (as illustrated in Figure 12):
resistive, capacitive, triboelectric, piezoelectric, and bioelectric coupling. Each of these sensing mechanisms
exhibit distinct characteristics. The resistive mechanism centers on the modulation of charge carrier transport
pathways. External stimuli can alter the geometric topology of the conductive network within the gel or affect
ionic mobility, with these microscopic changes ultimately manifesting as variations in overall resistance[49].

Benefiting from the high water content of hydrogels and their structural similarity to biological tissues, this
mechanism achieves high-fidelity conversion of physiological bioelectrical signals into electronic currents in
artificial circuits through ultra-low interfacial impedance[314].
Capitalizing on these mechanisms and leveraging their tissue-mimicking modulus and superior
biocompatibility, hydrogels not only resolve the mechanical mismatch at the biotic–abiotic interface but also
serve as a pivotal interactive medium bridging the physical world with digital systems. In this section, the
diverse applications of hydrogel sensors are categorized into four primary domains: pressure sensors, which
enhance force perception precision via modulus regulation and energy dissipation; strain sensors, which
achieve broader detection ranges and higher sensitivities through hydrogel integration; and environmental

5.1. Pressure sensors
Pressure sensors, as a critical branch in the field of flexible sensors, have garnered extensive attention and
research. Based on their working mechanisms, hydrogel-based pressure sensors can be further classified into
piezoresistive[320, 340–343], piezocapacitive[4, 321, 344, 345], triboelectric[43, 139, 322, 346], piezoelectric[323, 324, 347], and
piezoionic sensors[325, 326, 348–350].
Hydrogels exhibit exceptional flexibility and stretchability, enabling them to accommodate complex
deformation environments. This characteristic allows hydrogel-based stress sensors to conform to intricate
surfaces (such as human skin or mechanical joints) and undergo uniform deformation under external forces,
thereby achieving high-precision detection of stress distribution[351]. The combination of rigid conductive
polymer networks with entangled soft polymer chains was implemented to establish mechanically robust
hydrogels[327]. Specifically, AM and PVA were selected to construct a dual-network architecture crosslinked
by MBA. As shown in Figure 13(a), the hydrogel-based pressure sensors exhibited reliable piezoresistive
behavior under dynamic pressures (3.33, 5.02, and 6.67 kPa) and were employed to monitor diverse human
physiological activities, such as vocalization, swallowing processes, finger movements, and limb activities.
Ionic hydrogels have played a pivotal role in flexible pressure sensors due to their high ionic conductivity,
flexibility, self-healing properties, and biocompatibility. When a hydrogel-based pressure sensor is subjected
to external pressure, the 3D crosslinked network of the hydrogel undergoes compression. Such structural
modifications significantly shorten ion migration pathways and increase local electric field intensity, thereby
inducing alterations in electrical performance. During this process, the electric double layer (EDL) mechanism
plays a pivotal role[328, 352–354]. When the hydrogel interfaces with electrodes, an EDL structure spontaneously
forms at the contact boundary, wherein free ions within the hydrogel redistribute under electric fields to
establish Stern and diffuse layers. Upon pressure application, hydrogel compression modulates the charge
distribution profiles, consequently inducing interfacial capacitance/resistance variations. This EDL-governed
electromechanical coupling enables ionic hydrogel pressure sensors to achieve pressure detection with
enhanced sensitivity and rapid response time, simultaneously unveiling novel pathways for developing high-
performance flexible electronics with biomimetic sensing capabilities. For instance, a micro-dome dielectric
hydrogel (LSHM) utilising a sulphonated lignin (LS)-Fe3+ autocatalytic system was employed to construct a
capacitive pressure sensor (SCPS)[321]. Benefiting from the LSHM’s outstanding mechanical properties and
elastic recovery rate, the SCPS demonstrated a broad detection range and high sensitivity. As illustrated in

applied pressure causes asymmetric redistribution of mobile ions (e.g., Na+ and Cl⁻) within the hydrated

monitoring and served as a tactile nerve system for analgesic patients to prevent injuries.

5.2. Strain sensors
Hydrogels have been extensively investigated and established as premier candidates for high-performance
flexible strain sensors[197, 331, 332]. Operating primarily through piezoresistive or capacitive mechanisms, these
sensors transduce mechanical stimuli into electrical signals via geometric deformation or the reconfiguration
of internal conductive networks. Compared with traditional rigid sensors limited by narrow strain ranges (<5%)
and dry elastomer-based devices prone to interfacial noise, hydrogels demonstrate superior sensing
capabilities. The unique solid‒liquid hybrid state endows these sensors with an ultra-wide linear detection
range (often exceeding 1 000%) and exceptional fracture resistance, enabling comprehensive monitoring from
subtle pulse vibrations to large-scale joint movements. Meanwhile, the ionic transport mechanism circumvents
the percolation threshold failures common in dry conductive composites, ensuring superior signal linearity
and stability even under extreme deformation. Furthermore, the ultra-soft, conformal interface eliminates
contact resistance fluctuations (motion artifacts) during dynamic activities, significantly enhancing the SNR
and the limit of detection for minute stimuli.
To maintain signal stability and linearity over ultra-large strain ranges, ionic conductive hydrogels based
on a nanoclay physical interlocking mechanism have been developed[333]. This nano-reinforced
interpenetrating network endows the material with superior structural–mechanical–electrical integrity,
allowing the internal conductive pathways to reorganize stably even under substantial deformation.
Consequently, high-fidelity and reliable sensing performance is achieved. Leveraging this robustness, the
sensor can intimately conform to the dynamically beating heart surface, enabling not only the sensitive capture
of strain signals but also the accurate localization of myocardial infarction areas, demonstrating significant
potential for monitoring pathological physiological changes.
Traditional conductive hydrogels typically exhibit intrinsic isotropy in their structure and function, as
they are synthesized through the homogeneous polymerization of monomers. This structural characteristic
sharply contrasts with the highly ordered anisotropic architecture observed in biological soft tissues (e.g.,
muscles, tendons, and cartilage). To simulate this anisotropic structure, an anisotropic conductive hydrogel
with a direction-oriented polymer network was constructed by crosslinking PVA, PPy-decorated cellulose
nanofibres, and TA[330]. The hydrogel exhibited outstanding mechanical performance, with a tensile strength

5.4. Bioelectric sensors
Hydrogels have emerged as ideal candidates for flexible bioelectrode materials due to their inherent flexibility,
biocompatibility, and adhesiveness. The low modulus enables conformal adhesion between flexible electrodes
and skin, mitigating biomechanical mismatch and relative motion at the electrode–tissue interface, thereby
ensuring stable signal acquisition. The exceptional biocompatibility prevents skin irritation or damage during
prolonged wear, making them suitable for medical health monitoring. The low interfacial impedance facilitates
high-accuracy transfer of weak physiological signals from tissues to electrodes with enhanced signal-to-noise
ratios. Meanwhile, their strong adhesion allows stable tissue to contact without additional adhesives,
effectively suppressing interference from extreme deformation, motion, or vibration while improving wearing
comfort. Furthermore, high transparency enables convenient electrode manipulation and long-term
observation while guaranteeing biosafety. These properties have garnered increasing attention for constructing
seamless and conformal skin‒electrode interfaces. To date, numerous hydrogel-based electrodes have been
implemented for detecting human physiological and biochemical information, including ECG[369, 370], EEG[371],
EMG[36], and electrooculogram (EOG)[372].
ECG signal, a physiological indicator of heart function, results from the heart’s electrical activity.
Originating from the sinoatrial node, atrial muscle, atrioventricular node, and His-Purkinje system, this
electrical activity regulates the heart’s rhythmic contractions and relaxations. In clinical settings, ECG
monitoring is vital for diagnosing cardiovascular issues such as arrhythmia, myocardial ischemia, and
infarctions, as it can detect abnormalities in waveforms such as the P wave, QRS complex, and T wave.
Beyond diagnosis, ECG monitoring is also valuable for heart surgery, rehabilitation, and exercise physiology
studies, offering insights into heart function, guiding exercise regimens, and tracking cardiac health. For
instance, researchers have developed an ionic hydrogel from PVA, branched polyethyleneimine, and CaCl2 to
record ECG signals[35]. This non-covalently cross-linked network hydrogel featured 1 291% stretchability,
3.09 S·m⁻1 conductivity, strong adhesion, antibacterial properties, and recyclability. The temperature-sensitive

EMG, and EEG signals with high fidelity, high signal-to-noise ratio, and ultralow detection limits, showing
promise in healthcare electronics. For instance, the system could distinguish ECG signal differences between
male and female subjects during rest and post-exercise conditions using epidermal electrodes.

which exhibits a tissue-like modulus and exceptional flexibility, has been employed for monitoring EEGs[34].
PDA nanoparticles (PDA-NPs) obtained through PDA peroxidation were incorporated into the hydrogel,

5.5. Challenges in the practical application of hydrogel-based sensors
5.5.1. Long-term stability. At the sensor level, long-term unreliability, manifested as signal baseline drift and
dynamic response distortion, represents a primary bottleneck for practical applications. First, the stability of
the electrochemical interface under bias voltage remains unclear. During prolonged or dynamic loading, the
electrical double layer at the electrode/gel interface is susceptible to ion depletion[373] or electrochemical
reactions[303]. These processes cause interfacial impedance drift, leading to baseline fluctuations and a reduced
signal-to-noise ratio. Second, the intrinsic viscoelasticity of hydrogels induces mechanical hysteresis, which
compromises dynamic response fidelity. Such hysteretic behavior not only distorts dynamic signal waveforms

5.5.2. In-vivo biocompatibility. In implantable applications, long-term biocompatibility and functional
stability constitute the most formidable barriers to clinical translation. First, the foreign body reaction triggered
by the implant, including non-specific protein absorption and macrophage accumulation, can isolate the sensor
from the physiological environment for material exchange, leading to signal drift or even complete failure[374].
Second, for hydrogels that are degradable or contain nanofillers (such as CPs or metal nanowires), their
degradation kinetics and the long-term biological effects of their metabolic byproducts remain unclear[375].
The long-term retention or release of these nanofillers in the body may induce chronic inflammation or
unforeseen cytotoxicity. Therefore, achieving long-term stable operation of implantable sensors requires not
only that the material itself possesses bioinert or controlled degradation properties but also the design of anti-
fouling surfaces, controlled drug-release interfaces, and encapsulation strategies that ensure long-term sealing
at the device level.
5.5.3. Multi-signal crosstalk. Signal crosstalk under multi-field coupling and environmental interference
significantly compromises the measurement accuracy and selectivity of hydrogel-based sensors. These sensors
typically transduce physical (pressure, strain, and temperature) or chemical (humidity, ions, and biomolecules)
stimuli into resistance or capacitance changes within their bulk phase or at interfaces. However, hydrogels are
inherently sensitive to environmental fluctuations, making target signals susceptible to interference from non-
specific physical fields[376]. This multi-physics coupling effect is further amplified in complex real-world
environments, such as the surface of human skin. Therefore, addressing this challenge requires a dual approach.
The first involves material design, such as introducing functional components insensitive to specific
stimuli[377]. The second relies on signal processing, including the development of multi-parameter
synchronous acquisition and decoupling algorithms[378]. Achieving effective shielding or active compensation
of environmental noise, such as temperature and humidity variations, is essential for enhancing the detection
accuracy of hydrogel-based sensors in practical scenarios.

6. Conclusions and perspectives
This review establishes a comprehensive framework spanning fabrication methodologies, performance
regulation, assembly design, and device applications to systematically summarize the research progress on
hydrogel-based flexible sensors. First, advanced manufacturing processes, including solution processing,
microstructure molding, photolithography, additive manufacturing, and fiber spinning, are elucidated as the
cornerstones for realizing device structure customization. Furthermore, feasible strategies are revealed for
constructing efficient conductive networks, extreme environmental adaptability, such as anti-freezing and
water retention, self-healing capabilities, and biocompatibility, along with antibacterial properties. To address
the integration leap from pure materials to high-performance devices, this review summarizes chemical
anchoring interconnection techniques at heterogeneous interfaces and advanced encapsulation strategies.
These are key engineering pathways to solve device-level delamination failure and guarantee mechanical
integrity and environmental resistance. The deep integration of these materials and engineering technologies
collectively endows hydrogels with broad application potential in fields such as pressure and strain sensing,
environmental sensing, and bioelectric sensing. Finally, looking ahead, as shown in Figure 15, despite
significant progress in existing research, the following challenges remain to be addressed in this field:
(1) Signal decoupling and interference elimination
A major core challenge faced by hydrogel-based sensors in practical applications is their inherent
multidimensional cross-sensitivity. This frequently results in complex signal crosstalk (particularly baseline
drift induced by temperature and humidity) and pronounced viscoelastic hysteresis effects, thereby reducing
measurement reliability. To address this challenge, existing solutions primarily fall into two categories: passive
compensation and active decoupling. In terms of material and structural design, researchers aim to achieve
specific responses to individual physical quantities. For instance, composite materials with opposite thermal
response characteristics are employed to offset temperature interference[379] or strain-isolation structures such
as island-bridge configurations are used to eliminate coupling from mechanical signals[380, 381]. In back-end
signal processing, AI algorithms demonstrate strong decoupling potential, enabling feature extraction from
mixed signals and enabling independent quantification of multimodal stimuli[382]. However, most current
decoupling techniques can only distinguish between two types of stimuli, making them inadequate for dealing
with the complex multi-physics interference present in real-world environments. The highly specific ion
transport mechanisms of biological sensory receptors (such as mechano-gated and thermosensitive channels
in the skin) provide key inspiration for next-generation decoupling strategies. By constructing anisotropic

eliminating interference at its source, achieving high-dimensional, low-energy, and crosstalk-free sensing akin
to biological systems.
(2) Large-scale fabrication and standardization
Current laboratory-scale technologies (such as molding and single-nozzle printing) struggle to meet the
industrial’s stringent demands for high throughput, cost-effectiveness, and device consistency. Transitioning
from laboratory prototypes to factory-ready products requires not only the adoption of continuous
manufacturing processes like roll-to-roll processing or high-speed screen printing, but also an urgent need for
innovation in the manufacturing paradigm itself. With respect to the preparation strategy, the traditional trial-
and-error approach to formulation exploration is costly and inefficient. The introduction of emerging tools
such as AI is poised to reshape this process, steering hydrogel preparation strategies towards a data-driven
transformation. Through machine learning algorithms, researchers can swiftly screen vast datasets to identify
the optimal precursor formulations for desired performance combinations[383]. Second, in device fabrication,
developing integrated multi-material continuous manufacturing technologies is key to avoiding interface
defects caused by stepwise assembly. Continuous multi-material integrated 3D printing based on DIW has
been developed for the in-situ heterogeneous integration of functional hydrogels, conductive electrodes, and
encapsulation materials[384, 385]. Notably, the rheological properties of hydrogel inks are highly sensitive to
environmental conditions, serving as a critical factor in determining printability[386]. Future research should
extend beyond automation with fixed parameters and focus on incorporating feedback loops enabled by
computer vision and machine learning[387]. By developing intelligent closed-loop control systems capable of
monitoring ink status in real time and dynamically adjusting printing parameters, rigid open-loop processes
can be replaced, fundamentally addressing batch-to-batch variability and ensuring the yield and reliability of
large-scale production.
(3) System-level closed-loop integration and energy autonomy
To overcome the reliance on bulky external power supplies and computational units, hydrogel-based
sensors must evolve from passive sensing terminals to autonomous intelligent systems capable of “sensing-
decision-feedback” functionality. Regarding energy and self-driven sensing, although self-powered hydrogel
devices based on TENG/PENG have achieved preliminary integration of energy and sensing[388–390], their

capability. Inspired by the mechanically gated ion migration mechanisms within skin mechanoreceptors, the
emerging piezoionic effect offers a highly promising new pathway[350, 391]. This quasi-DC output characteristic,
which is based on ion migration, not only enables more stable self-driven sensing but also has potential for
enhancing energy harvesting and management efficiency through coupling with double-layer capacitance. In
terms of information processing, while embedded AI and edge computing enable low-latency data
processing[392], the significant modulus mismatch between conventional silicon-based circuits and soft
hydrogels remains the foremost obstacle to integration. A more forward-looking approach involves
establishing neuromorphic computing architectures based on ion-electronics. By constructing artificial
synapses or ionic logic gates, signals can be processed and stored in situ directly using ion flows within the
hydrogel[393]. This bio‑inspired paradigm of synchronous sensing‑computation is expected to fundamentally
eliminate the energy‑consumption bottleneck of analog‑to‑digital conversion, thereby contributing to the
development of highly integrated, wireless, and untethered next‑generation soft intelligent terminals.
(4) Device-level reliability under dynamic service
Under dynamic service conditions, a significant gap remains between material stability (e.g., resistance
to dehydration) and device-level reliability. To address signal distortions caused by mechanisms such as
mechanical fatigue, electrochemical polarization drift, and interfacial delamination, a paradigm shift toward
comprehensive reliability assurance is imperative. At the material level, constructing highly dissipative,
fatigue-resistant networks is the foundational step. Researchers have identified multiple implementation
strategies, such as utilizing sacrificial bonds within multi-network structures to dissipate energy through bond
rupture[394] or incorporating porous frameworks (e.g., covalent organic frameworks, COFs) to form molecular-
scale mechanically interlocked networks, where the confined sliding of polymer chains within nanochannels
enables efficient energy dissipation[395]. A more forward-looking approach involves integrating dynamic
covalent bonds or supramolecular interactions to achieve in situ self-healing[396], allowing devices to
autonomously repair micro-cracks at their inception, thereby fundamentally combating mechanical fatigue. At
the interface level, integrated construction strategies based on topological interlocking or modulus gradient
designs offer a viable path to mitigate delamination during dynamic operation[397]. Concurrently, replacing
purely electric double-layer capacitance with Faradaic processes[398] can establish non-polarized interfaces,
thereby suppressing potential drift during long-term operation. Finally, in terms of evaluation, there is an
